transcript.text: Hi, my Hotpoint Aquarius dryer is taking forever to dry and the top gets really hot. Model is TCM580GUK if that helps

From what you have described, the most likely cause is clean the lint filter and the condenser/heat exchanger. A blocked lint filter stops the airflow, and many dryers then cut the heat to stop overheating. Clean the fluff filter in the door opening (heat-pump models often have a second one at the bottom too). Was it full of fluff (and is it clean now), or was it already clean?
It was quite full, with a thick layer of fluff, I'm afraid I do sometimes forget to clean it. I should also mention that the top of the dryer gets very hot, and I often run it while I'm out at work.

From what you have described, the most likely cause is the lint filter. Behind the flap at the bottom front there's a condenser unit (or a second filter on heat-pump models). Take it out and rinse the fluff off under the tap, then let it drip-dry and refit it. Was it clogged with fluff (and is it clean now), or was it already clean?
Yes, the condenser unit had lint packed on the fins. I've rinsed it and it looks much cleaner now. Is there anything else I should check, given how hot the top of the dryer gets?

Yes, you should check that the air intake grille on the front door is not blocked by lint or clothing. Also ensure the exhaust vent at the back of the machine is clear and not kinked, as restricted airflow causes overheating and poor drying performance. From what you have described, the most likely cause is clean the lint/fluff filter (and condenser filter) and clear the airflow. Damp laundry is most often an airflow problem, and the first free check is the fluff filter in the door opening — heat-pump models often have a second filter at the bottom too. Was it full of fluff (and is it clean now), is the mesh torn, or was it already clean?
[Helpful to see: image "Where the lint filter is" — The fluff/lint filter sits in the door opening or just inside the rim. Lift it out and clear the fluff after every load. Typical layout — your dryer may differ.]

Thank you. I've already told you the door filter had a thick layer of fluff, and the condenser unit is now rinsed. I'm not sure where the air intake grille you mention is, or how to check it. Is there anything else I should look at, or is it safe to keep using the dryer while I'm out at work?

You should stop using the tumble dryer until you have cleaned the air intake grille, as restricted airflow causes overheating and poor drying performance. It is not safe to leave an appliance running unattended for extended periods due to fire risk. From what you have described, the most likely cause is blocked airflow tripping the overheat cut-out. Check the vent hose out of the back: it should be short, without kinks or squashed sections, and clear of fluff all the way to the outside vent. Was it kinked, squashed or blocked (and is it sorted), or was it already clear?

I'm afraid I'm not sure what vent hose you mean, as mine is a condenser model and I wouldn't know where to look for one. I'll stop running it while I'm out. Is there anything else I should check, or should I get someone to look at it?

You should clean the air intake grille, which is usually located behind a panel on the back of the machine. If drying times do not improve after this and ensuring the condenser is dry, you will need to get a professional to look at it. Run a normal heat programme again for 10–15 minutes. Is it heating now, or still cold?
I haven't been able to find an air intake grille on the back, so I haven't cleaned one. I did run it for 10 minutes though, and yes, it is heating. The top panel still gets very hot.
From what you have checked, this needs an appliance engineer to look at it: the next steps are beyond the checks that are safe to do yourself.
